Updates

Project updates

September 23, 2026

A restored match returns to the exact decision

We created and retained a current-version backup containing two real engine fixtures: one match paused during a block and another played all the way to full time. The backup was restored into a separate, empty local database with separate storage. Accounts, memberships, frozen teams, requests, checkpoints, the completed result, and all 42 recorded replay states matched the source before the restored application accepted traffic.

The paused match explains the similar-looking version numbers. Game revision 13 means thirteen authoritative decisions had been accepted. Recovery generation 14 means fourteen durable checkpoints existed, starting with the initial state. After the restored engine applied the only legal push square, those became revision 14 and checkpoint generation 15. Both original players then resumed the match in separate signed-in browsers: Home could choose Follow or Do Not Follow, while Away saw the same position without an action.

The other labels describe different compatibility layers. Database schema 6 is the current storage layout; runtime r4.1 is the current active-match recovery behavior; recovery format 3 is the checkpoint structure; and replay format 1 is the completed-history structure. Keeping these identities separate lets restore reject the wrong database, application, checkpoint, or replay combination instead of guessing.

The completed match is intact at final revision 41, checkpoint generation 42, with 42 replay states. One acceptance item remains open: the current authenticated browser protocol lists active games but does not expose completed results or replay. The data passed direct restore checks, but we are not claiming the completed replay was viewed through the live UI or that this is public-service readiness.

September 23, 2026

Where the M4 service work stands

M4 has turned the earlier two-player game proof into a versioned service foundation around the existing authoritative Java BB2025 engine. The current stack combines Java and Maven, MariaDB persistence, a React/Vite browser, scoped Firebase identities, frozen team inputs, durable active-match recovery, bounded resident sessions, and manifest-bound backup and restore.

The important boundary is that the server still owns membership, legal actions, dice, retries, and mutation order. Browser input cannot select a role or private state, and an exact retry is reconciled from durable history instead of running the game action twice.

M4 is still an active reliability milestone, not a launch announcement. The completed-replay browser surface, broader end-to-end load evidence, storage operations, and remaining deployment gates stay separate. Local and DEV checks do not establish production capacity or public-service readiness.

September 21, 2026

R4: making room without losing the match

R4 added lifecycle limits around recovered games. Completed engines leave the in-memory resident pool only after their result is durable. Idle active engines can leave memory while their checkpoints remain available, failed recovery stays failed closed, and a full pool rejects a new activation before it changes stored state.

The resident limit remains 32 engines, and new retained checkpoint identities are capped at 1,024. Those limits do not delete old games or weaken exact retries. Repeatable local workloads completed 34 native BB2025 matches per run, including full-time release, reconnect, lost-acknowledgement retry, and slow-client protection, while preserving the single-worker mutation model.

This measured a serial local workload and bounded failure fixtures. It did not prove 32 simultaneous live matches, maximum-size checkpoints, network latency, automatic disk cleanup, or production capacity.

September 21, 2026

R3: real identities with deliberately small views

R3 connected the game service to real Firebase identities and replaced client-selected roles with server-side account scopes and persisted match membership. Invitations, reconnects, player actions, spectator reads, and retries are authorized again at the point of use. A newer connection also replaces an older connection for the same account instead of leaving two competing sessions.

The browser receives only the information required for its role. Players remain labelled You and Opponent, spectators see neutral Home and Away labels, and extra identity, credential, checkpoint, dice, or ownership fields are rejected before rendering. Exact Host, Origin, project, and WebSocket route policies keep local and DEV configurations separated.

The verified surface covers players, active-game spectators, preparation, teams, and gameplay. Administration, legacy routes, completed results, and replay were intentionally left unavailable. DEV and local evidence did not make a production-readiness claim.

September 17, 2026

Two players, one secure session

The first multiplayer proof is now working on DEV. Two separately signed-in players can create and join a private session, see each other arrive and reconnect, and share a simple ordered chat log.

Google sign-in and email-link sign-in both lead straight into play. The game service accepts a fresh Firebase token only after the encrypted WebSocket connection opens, verifies it against the matching Firebase project, and keeps player identities private behind the familiar labels “You” and “Opponent.”

This is deliberately a small step: no teams, rules, matchmaking, spectators, or FUMBBL-account access. It gives us a tested foundation for building the game experience together.

September 2026

Repository integration

The project site, browser client, and Firebase Hosting assembly are now separated into independently buildable components. This change does not alter the existing Java game engine or FUMBBL accounts.
